title: Monday: "How was your weekend?"
rule: Answer with a feeling word plus one real detail, then hand it back.

examples.work:
Arjun: "How was your weekend?"
You: "Lazy, in a good way. I finally watched Kantara. Yours?"
examples.everyday:
Neighbour: "Busy weekend?"
You: "Very. My nephew's birthday, twenty kids. Did you go out?"

analogy: A detail is the biscuit with the chai: it gives them something to pick up.
tryPrompt: Monday, 9:30, at the coffee machine. Fatima asks, "How was your weekend?" Answer for real.
answer: Tiring but fun. We drove to Mysore for my cousin's housewarming. Did you do anything nice?
credit: The Reveal step in Carol Fleming's ARE

title: Pick up their thread
rule: Comment on the one detail they gave, then ask about it.

examples.work:
Riya: "I was in Jaipur last week."
You: "Oh nice! Work or holiday?"
examples.everyday:
Cousin: "I've started running."
You: "Good for you! Mornings or evenings?"

analogy: Their detail is a loose thread. Pull it gently and more comes out.
tryPrompt: Joseph says, "I spent Sunday fixing my bike." Reply with one comment and one question about it.
answer: On your own? That's impressive. What was wrong with it?

title: "Busy week?" Answer first, then a hook
rule: Give the answer in your first word, then one detail and a question.

examples.work:
Manager: "Busy week?"
You: "Very. Two client demos. Is yours any calmer?"
examples.everyday:
Friend: "Coming tonight?"
You: "Can't, sorry. Mum's visiting. Sunday brunch instead?"

analogy: Like a cricket scoreboard: the score first, the story of the overs after.
tryPrompt: In the lift, a senior manager asks, "Busy week?" You launch the new app on Thursday. Answer in two sentences.
answer: Very busy. We launch the new app on Thursday. How's your week going?

title: A bad day, said lightly
rule: Be honest about a bad day, but keep it short and light.

examples.work:
Priya: "How's it going?"
You: "Long day. The build broke twice. Tea first, then round three!"
examples.everyday:
Dad: "How was work?"
You: "Rough, honestly. But I'm home, and I can smell dal."

analogy: Share the rain, not the whole weather report.
tryPrompt: Your client cancelled at the last minute today. A colleague asks, "How's your day?" Answer.
answer: A bit frustrating, honestly. The client cancelled at the last minute. How's yours going?

title: Hand it back with "catch up"
rule: Give one detail, then hand it back using "catch up".

examples.work:
Rahul: "Good break?"
You: "Great. Two days in Coorg, zero emails. Let's catch up on what I missed."
examples.everyday:
Old friend: "It's been ages!"
You: "It has! I've changed jobs since. Shall we catch up over chai this week?"

analogy: Like a rally in badminton: your shot's done, now it's theirs.
tryPrompt: You're back from a week's leave. Your teammate says, "Welcome back!" Reply with a detail, then use "catch up".
answer: Thanks! Goa was lovely, lots of fish curry. Can we catch up after lunch?

title: Match their mood
rule: Meet their energy first: excited with excited, tired with gentle.

examples.work:
Arjun: "We finally shipped it!"
You: "Yes! Three months of work. How are you celebrating?"
examples.everyday:
Friend (quietly): "Long week."
You: "Sounds like it. Want to just get chai and sit?"

analogy: Like joining a song: match the tempo before you sing your part.
tryPrompt: Riya rushes in: "I passed my driving test!" Reply in two or three sentences.
answer: Congratulations! That's huge. Was it your first try?

title: Today in three parts: what, but, so
rule: Tell one thing from today: what happened, "but…", "so…".

examples.work: I planned to finish the report early, but the Wi-Fi went down. So I finished it offline and sent it at lunch.
examples.everyday: I wanted a quiet Sunday, but the plumber came at nine. So we had brunch at noon.

analogy: A train journey: the plan, a red signal, then the new route.
tryPrompt: Think of one plan from today that didn't go as expected. Tell it with "but" and "so".
answer: I wanted to leave the office at six, but my manager called a quick meeting at 5:55. So I ate my dinner on the bus home.
credit: South Park writers' "but / therefore" rule, built into Randy Olson's ABT

title: Tell it with two words from this week
rule: Tell one moment from today, using two of this week's words.

examples.work: We ran into a problem with the login at noon, but Riya sorted it out in ten minutes.
examples.everyday: Our Sunday picnic got pushed back a week, so we caught up over chai at home instead.

analogy: New words are new spices: use them in today's cooking, or they sit in the jar.
tryPrompt: Tell one moment from today in under 30 seconds. Use two of: run into, sort out, push back, follow up.
answer: This morning we ran into a problem: the client's file wouldn't open, and the call was in ten minutes. I asked Fatima, and she sorted it out in two. We started on time.

title: End with what changed
rule: End with what changed: in the situation, or in you.

examples.work: I used to dread client calls. Today's went well, and now I'm looking forward to Friday's.
examples.everyday: I thought my landlord was rude. Then he fixed our geyser at midnight. Now I bring him sweets.

analogy: A story is a before-and-after photo. Without the "after", it's just a photo.
tryPrompt: Think of something you did differently this week. Say what you thought before, what happened, and how you see it now.
answer: I always took the 8:30 bus and reached late. On Monday I missed it and walked to the metro instead. I reached ten minutes early. Now I take the metro every day.

title: Result first, then the moment
rule: Say the result in one line, then tell the moment it happened.

examples.work: The demo went fine in the end. Two minutes in, the screen froze.
examples.everyday: We made the train, just. The auto stopped dead on the flyover.

analogy: A cricket score first, then the one over everyone talks about.
tryPrompt: Your manager asks, "What happened with the demo?" It crashed, but you fixed it live. Result first, then the moment.
answer: It went well in the end. Two minutes in, the screen froze and the client went quiet. I restarted the app and said, "Live demos, right?" They laughed. Ten minutes later, they asked about pricing.

title: Add one line someone said
rule: Put in one real line someone said, in their exact words.

examples.work: My manager read the deck, looked up and said, "Who wrote slide nine?"
examples.everyday: The auto driver turned round and said, "Sir, change is your problem, not mine."

analogy: A quote is a voice note inside your story: they hear the person, not just you.
tryPrompt: Tell a moment from this week when someone said something that surprised you. Include their exact words.
answer: I was rushing out with my laptop still open, and the security guard said, "Sir, the laptop will reach before you." I laughed all the way to the lift.

title: Swap the general word for the real one
rule: Name the real thing: "Activa", not "vehicle"; "dosa", not "food".

examples.work: I rode my Activa to the client's office in Whitefield.
examples.everyday: We grabbed masala dosas at the stall outside the station.

insteadOf: I took my vehicle and went to eat some food.
analogy: General words are a pencil sketch; real names add the colour.
tryPrompt: Tell what you had for lunch yesterday, and where. Use at least two real names.
answer: Yesterday I had rajma chawal at the Punjabi place near our office. The owner gave me extra onions without asking.

title: Yes or no in your first word
rule: Start with yes or no, then give one reason.

examples.work: No, not today. Testing needs one more day.
examples.everyday: Yes, I'll come. I'll be there by eight.

insteadOf: Actually, the vendor was late, and testing took time, so maybe not…
analogy: Like an umpire: the finger goes up or not, before any explanation.
tryPrompt: Your manager asks, "Can you take the Thursday client call?" You can, but only after 3 p.m.
answer: Yes, after 3 p.m. I'm in a review till then.

title: Point first, with a sharp verb
rule: Give the point first, with a sharp verb like "fixed" or "flagged".

examples.work: We fixed the login bug. It's been live since ten.
examples.everyday: I booked the tickets. The train's at six tomorrow.

insteadOf: So regarding the bug, we did some work on it and it's done.
analogy: A sharp verb is a sharp knife: one clean cut, no sawing.
tryPrompt: In stand-up, report that you found a mistake in the invoice and told finance yesterday.
answer: I found an error in the invoice and flagged it to finance yesterday.

title: One point per sentence
rule: Break the long sentence; give each point its own sentence.

examples.work: The build failed. Rahul is on leave. I'll fix it by Friday.
examples.everyday: The cab's late. It's raining. Start dinner without me.

insteadOf: The build failed and Rahul is on leave and the client wants it by Friday and…
analogy: Like train coaches: each carries its own load, linked but separate.
tryPrompt: Tell your team three things: the server is slow, IT knows, and it will be fixed by lunch.
answer: The server's slow today. IT knows about it. They'll fix it by lunch.

title: "What do you do?" in one line
rule: Answer "What do you do?" in one line, then hand it back.

examples.work: I build the app that small shops use for billing. What about you?
examples.everyday: I make apps for small shops. How about you?

insteadOf: So basically I joined in 2019, then moved teams, and now I'm handling…
analogy: A one-line answer is a shop's signboard: they know what's inside before walking in.
tryPrompt: At a friend's wedding, someone asks, "So, what do you do?" Answer in one line, then hand it back.
answer: I help small shops take payments on their phones. How about you?

title: Say it in half the words
rule: Cut the warm-up; keep only what the listener needs.

examples.work: The meeting's moved to four.
examples.everyday: Dinner's at eight now, not seven.

insteadOf: So basically what I wanted to say is that the meeting has been moved.
analogy: Like packing a cabin bag: only what you'll actually use.
tryPrompt: Say this in under 10 words: "I just wanted to let you all know that the office will be closed on Friday."
answer: The office is closed on Friday.

title: Buy time, then answer
rule: Use a short phrase to think, then give the point.

examples.work: Good question. Short answer: yes, by Friday.
examples.everyday: Let me think… the blue one.

analogy: Like a bowler's run-up: a few steps first, then the delivery.
tryPrompt: In a meeting, someone asks how many users signed up last week. You need a second to recall it.
answer: Good question. Let me think… about twelve hundred last week.

title: Move it earlier: "bring forward"
rule: To move a plan earlier, "bring it forward".

examples.work: Can we bring the review forward to Tuesday?
examples.everyday: Let's bring dinner forward to seven; the match starts at eight.

analogy: Like moving your ticket to an earlier train.
tryPrompt: The client wants Friday's demo on Wednesday instead. Tell your team.
answer: The client wants to bring the demo forward to Wednesday.

title: Chase politely: "follow up"
rule: To check again on something pending, "follow up on" it.

examples.work: I'll follow up with Priya on the contract today.
examples.everyday: Did you follow up with the landlord about the leak?

analogy: A second knock on the door, a little later, still polite.
tryPrompt: You emailed the vendor on Monday; no reply yet. Tell your manager what you'll do today.
answer: No reply yet, so I'll follow up with them today.

title: "Leave it with me", then a time
rule: Say "Leave it with me" to take a task on.

examples.work: "Can someone check the numbers?" "Leave it with me. I'll send them by four."
examples.everyday: "Who'll call the plumber?" "Leave it with me."

analogy: Like taking the keys from someone's hand: now it's yours to drive.
tryPrompt: Your manager asks who can fix the broken client link before lunch. Take it, answer first, and give a time.
answer: Leave it with me. I'll have it fixed by twelve.

title: Raise a concern, calmly
rule: Say "I'd like to raise a concern" to flag a worry politely.

examples.work: I'd like to raise a concern about the Friday deadline.
examples.everyday: I raised a concern with the school about the bus timing.

analogy: Like raising your hand in class: polite, visible, and everyone pauses.
tryPrompt: In the planning meeting, you worry the team is too small for two launches. Say it politely.
answer: I'd like to raise a concern: we may not have enough people for two launches.

title: "Heavy traffic" in a real reply
rule: Use "heavy traffic" in a 1+1 reply, then hand it back.

examples.work:
Priya: "Rough morning?"
You: "Heavy traffic on the flyover. An hour! How was your commute?"
examples.everyday:
Mum: "Why so late?"
You: "Heavy traffic near the market. Have you eaten?"

analogy: A new word is a new shirt: wear it out once and it starts to feel like yours.
tryPrompt: You're 15 minutes late for a team lunch because of traffic. Arjun says, "There you are!" Reply.
answer: Sorry! Heavy traffic all the way from Indiranagar. Have you ordered yet?

title: Ask to be filled in
rule: "Fill someone in" means tell them what they missed.

examples.work: Can you fill me in on yesterday's client call?
examples.everyday: I missed the family call. Can you fill me in?

analogy: Like filling in the blank pages of their notebook.
tryPrompt: You missed the first half of the meeting. Afterwards, ask Rahul to tell you what happened.
answer: Rahul, could you fill me in on the first half?
